p.src: Now Dai Zong and Shi Xiu saw that the man was dressed like a government courier and appeared extremely flustered. Dai Zong asked, “What official business are you really on?” The man put down his chopsticks, wiped his mouth, and said to Dai Zong, “You know that Tian Hu has rebelled in Hebei, do you not?” Dai Zong replied, “We have heard a little of it.” The man said, “That scoundrel Tian Hu has seized prefectures and counties, and the imperial troops cannot withstand him. Recently he captured Gaizhou, and any day now he will attack Weizhou. The people inside the city live in terror day and night, while those outside have fled in every direction. That is why our prefecture has sent me to the provincial offices with an urgent dispatch requesting aid.” When he had finished, he rose, shouldered his bundle, took up his umbrella staff, hurriedly paid for his wine, and went out, sighing, “A man on official duty has no freedom at all. My wife and children are still in the city. Heaven above, if only relief troops are dispatched soon!” Then he lengthened his stride and hastened toward the capital.

p.src: Having learned this news, Dai Zong and Shi Xiu also paid for their wine, left the tavern, and returned to camp, where they reported the matter to Vanguard Song. Song Jiang consulted Wu Yong, saying, “It is most improper for all our commanders to remain here idle. We should petition the Son of Heaven and volunteer to lead our forces against the rebels.” Wu Yong said, “For this, Grand Marshal Su must first sponsor our petition.” They assembled the commanders at once to discuss the proposal, and all were delighted. The next day Song Jiang donned his official robes and led more than ten horsemen into the city, riding straight to the Grand Marshal’s residence before dismounting. The Grand Marshal happened to be at home, so Song Jiang had his arrival announced. When the Grand Marshal learned of it, he promptly ordered that Song Jiang be admitted. Song Jiang entered the hall, bowed twice, and offered the customary greetings. Grand Marshal Su asked, “General, what brings you here?” Song Jiang said, “My honored patron, I have heard that Tian Hu has rebelled in Hebei, occupied prefectures and commanderies, presumptuously instituted his own reign title, and advanced as far as Gaizhou; before long he will attack Weizhou. My troops and I have long been idle; we willingly offer to lead them forth, suppress the rebels, and serve our country with all our loyalty. I beg Your Excellency to sponsor our petition.” Grand Marshal Su was overjoyed to hear this. “You generals are so loyal and righteous, and willing to serve the state. I shall do everything in my power to recommend your request.” Song Jiang thanked him, saying, “My companions and I have repeatedly received Your Excellency’s great favor. Though it is engraved upon our hearts and carved into our bones, we have no way to repay it.” Grand Marshal Su then ordered wine to be laid out for his guest. In the evening Song Jiang returned to camp and informed all the chieftains.

p.src: Now the next morning Grand Marshal Su entered the palace for the court audience and found the emperor in the Hall of Fragrant Robes. Officials of the provincial ministries were reporting that Tian Hu had rebelled in Hebei, occupied five prefectures and fifty-six counties, established a reign title, and proclaimed himself king. He had now captured Lingzhou and Huaizhou, alarming the neighboring regions, which had submitted urgent dispatches. The emperor was greatly alarmed and asked his civil and military officials, “Which of you will exert himself on Our behalf and destroy these bandits?” Grand Marshal Su stepped out from the ranks of officials, held his court tablet before his breast, prostrated himself, and memorialized, “Your servant has heard that Tian Hu’s uprising, which began by cutting down trees for weapons and raising poles as banners, has now spread like wildfire. Without fierce generals and valiant troops, it will be difficult to suppress. Vanguard Song, victorious over Liao, is now encamped outside the capital. I beg Your Majesty to issue an edict and send this army to suppress the rebels; it will surely achieve great merit.” The emperor was delighted and immediately ordered officials of the ministries to leave the city under imperial command and summon Song Jiang and Lu Junyi. They were brought directly before the Hall of Fragrant Robes to have audience with the emperor. When they had completed their obeisances, the imperial voice declared, “We know that you are heroes of loyalty and honor. We now command you to campaign in Hebei; do not shrink from the hardship. Return soon with songs of victory, and We shall richly promote you.” Song Jiang and Lu Junyi kowtowed and memorialized, “Having received Your Majesty’s gracious trust, how could we fail to bend our every effort to the task and labor on until death!” The emperor’s countenance shone with pleasure. By edict he appointed Song Jiang Chief Vanguard for Pacifying the North and Lu Junyi Deputy Vanguard. Each was bestowed imperial wine, a golden belt, a brocade robe, golden armor, and colored silks. All the other senior and subordinate officers were awarded bolts of silk and silver. Once they reported that the rebels had been pacified, rewards and promotions would be granted according to merit, together with higher offices and titles. The unit commanders throughout the army were also granted silver, to be drawn from the imperial treasury. A date was fixed for the army to depart on campaign. Song Jiang and Lu Junyi bowed twice more in gratitude, received the imperial command, withdrew from court, mounted their horses, and returned to camp, where they took their seats in the command tent. They immediately assembled all the commanders and ordered everyone to prepare saddles, horses, clothing, and armor for the campaign against Tian Hu.

p.src: Now this Tian Hu of Hebei was a hunter from Qinyuan County in Weisheng Prefecture. He possessed great strength, was skilled in arms, and made a practice of associating with young ruffians. The region was ringed by countless mountains and well suited to gathering armed bands. Moreover, floods and droughts came in constant succession; the people were destitute, their resources exhausted, and their hearts inclined toward disorder. Seizing the opportunity, Tian Hu gathered desperate outlaws, fabricated sorcerous rumors, and incited the ignorant populace. At first they merely plundered some goods, but later they seized prefectures and counties, and the imperial troops dared not face their onslaught. But, you may ask, Tian Hu was no more than a hunter—how did he become so rampant? Listen, dear reader: in those days the civil officials craved money and the military officers feared death. Though every prefecture and county had troops assigned to its defense, their rolls were padded with fictitious names and those actually present were old and feeble. One man might draw the pay of two or three soldiers; or an idle servant from a powerful household might pay a dozen or so taels as a substitution fee, purchase a place on the rolls, and thereby collect rations and wages for his own use. When the roll was called or drills were held, they simply hired someone to answer in their stead. Superiors and subordinates covered for one another, forming an unbreakable web of deceit. The state exhausted its treasury yet gained not the slightest practical benefit. When battle came, they knew nothing of fighting. Whatever their rank or station, the moment they saw dust rising ahead and heard the guns roar, they wished only that their parents had given them two more legs. At the time several officers did lead troops in pursuit of Tian Hu, but how could they dare advance against him? They merely trailed behind him, rushing east and west in pursuit and making an empty show of force; they even killed innocent people and claimed credit for it. The people grew ever more resentful and instead joined the rebels to escape the imperial troops. Thus Tian Hu was able to occupy five prefectures and fifty-six counties. The first of these five prefectures was Weisheng, now known as Qinzhou; the second was Fenyang, now known as Fenzhou; the third was Zhaode, now known as Lu’an; the fourth was Jinning, now known as Pingyang; and the fifth was Gaizhou, now known as Zezhou. The fifty-six counties were all subordinate counties governed by these five prefectures. Tian Hu built palaces in Fenyang, set up a spurious administration of civil and military officials, palace ministers and field commanders, and ruled the region alone, styling himself the King of Jin. His troops were elite, his generals fierce, and the mountains and rivers of his territory forbidding. He had now divided his forces into two columns and sent them forth to invade.

p.src: Song Jiang’s commands were strict and clear, his ranks orderly and disciplined; wherever they passed, they took not so much as a hair from the people—this goes without saying. When the army reached the borders of Yuanwu County, the magistrate came out to the suburbs to welcome them. Scouts from the vanguard reported that the ships of their own chiefs were already waiting on the riverbank to ferry the army across. Song Jiang ordered Li Jun and the others to lead six hundred naval troops, divide them into two squadrons, and deploy one on either side. They also commandeered local boats to carry the horses, carts, and equipment. Song Jiang’s great army crossed in order to the northern bank of the Yellow River. He then ordered Li Jun and the others to command the warships and proceed to the Wei River at Weizhou to rendezvous with them.

p.src: The vanguard of Song Jiang’s army marched to Weizhou and encamped there. The officials of Weizhou laid out a banquet to await Vanguard Commander Song. When he arrived, they invited him into the city and entertained him, saying, “The rebel Tian Hu’s forces are vast; they must not be underestimated. Zezhou is held by Niu Wenzhong, Tian Hu’s false Commissioner of Military Affairs. He has sent his subordinates Zhang Xiang and Wang Zhi with ten thousand troops to attack Huixian, which belongs to this prefecture; and Shen An and Qin Sheng, with another ten thousand troops, have come to attack Wushe, a county under Huaizhou. We beg you, Vanguard Commander, to hasten to their relief!” After hearing them out, Song Jiang returned to camp and consulted Wu Yong about dispatching troops to the rescue. Wu Yong said, “Lingchuan is a strategic stronghold of Gaizhou. Better that we march straight upon Lingchuan; then the sieges of both counties will lift of themselves.” Lu Junyi immediately said, “Though I have little ability, I am willing to lead troops and take Lingchuan.” Song Jiang was delighted and assigned Lu Junyi ten thousand cavalry and five hundred infantry. The cavalry chiefs were Hua Rong, Qin Ming, Dong Ping, Suo Chao, Huang Xin, Sun Li, Yang Zhi, Shi Jin, Zhu Tong, and Mu Hong. The infantry chiefs were Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, Li Gun, Lu Zhishen, Wu Song, Liu Tang, Yang Xiong, and Shi Xiu.

p.src: The next day, Lu Junyi led his troops away. In his command tent, Song Jiang again discussed with Wu Yong the best plan for advancing the army. Wu Yong said, “The rebel troops have long grown arrogant. Vanguard Commander Lu is certain to succeed on this expedition. There is only one concern: the mountains and rivers of the Three Jin region are steep and perilous. We must have two chiefs go ahead as spies to learn the terrain before we can advance.” Before he had finished speaking, Yan Qing came to the front of the tent and reported, “There is no need for the military adviser to trouble himself. The lay of the mountains and rivers is already here.” Yan Qing then produced a handscroll and spread it out upon the table. Song Jiang and Wu Yong examined it carefully from beginning to end. It was a map of the mountains, rivers, cities, passes, and defiles of the Three Jin region. Every place suitable for encampment, ambush, or battle was recorded on it in meticulous detail. Wu Yong asked in astonishment, “Where did you obtain this map?” Yan Qing said to Song Jiang, “The other day, when we withdrew after defeating Liao and returned to Shuanglin Town, I met a man whose surname was Xu and whose personal name was Guanzhong. He invited me to his home and, when we parted, gave me this map. He called it nothing but a few clumsy strokes. After I returned to camp, I happened to take it out and examine it at leisure, and only then realized that it was a map of the Three Jin region.” Song Jiang said, “When you returned the other day, we were in the midst of preparing for the imperial audience, and in all the bustle I never asked you for the details. This man seems a true hero. You have often spoken well of him to me. What is he doing now?” Yan Qing replied, “Guanzhong is learned and gifted, skilled in arms, and brave and loyal. As for lesser arts—music, chess, alchemy, and painting—there is not one he does not understand.” He then recounted in full how Guanzhong had no wish to take office, lived in seclusion in the mountains, and everything they had said to each other. Wu Yong said, “He is truly a thoughtful man of the realm.” Song Jiang and Wu Yong sighed in admiration and praised him without cease.

p.src: Now Lu Junyi, having taken command of the troops, first ordered Huang Xin and Sun Li to lead three thousand men and lie in ambush five li east of Lingchuan, while Shi Jin and Yang Zhi led another three thousand to lie in ambush five li west of the city. “At the fifth watch tonight, gag your horses’ bits, remove the bells, and each party steal quietly into position. From the eastern ranks, Hua Rong rode out with his spear leveled and engaged him. They fought for more than thirty bouts without either gaining the upper hand. By the drawbridge, Shen Ji saw that Dong Cheng could not prevail. Brandishing his polished steel spear, he urged his horse forward to join the fight. Seeing the two men close upon him from either side, Hua Rong wheeled his horse and fled east. Dong Cheng and Shen Ji pressed close behind him, whereupon Hua Rong turned his horse and fought them again.

p.src: From atop the city wall, Geng Gong saw Dong Cheng and Shen Ji give chase. Fearing that something might go wrong, he was just about to sound the drums to recall them. Suddenly, a fierce detachment burst from the Song ranks—Li Kui, Lu Zhishen, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, and more than a dozen other leaders. They flew across the drawbridge with such speed that the northern troops, unable to withstand their ferocity, could not stop them. Geng Gong urgently ordered the gates shut. But no sooner was the command spoken than Lu Zhishen and Li Kui had already stormed into the city. The gate guards surged forward together, but Zhishen gave a mighty roar and felled two of them with one sweep of his monk’s staff. Li Kui swung his axes and cut down five or six men. Bao Xu and the others poured in behind them. They seized the city gate and scattered its defenders. Seeing that the situation had turned against him, Geng Gong scrambled down and tried to flee north, but the infantry overtook and captured him alive.

p.src: Dong Cheng and Shen Ji were still fighting Hua Rong when they heard shouting arise by the drawbridge. They hurriedly wheeled their horses and galloped back. Hua Rong did not pursue them. Instead, he secured his steel spear in its saddle-ring, took up his bow, and drew an arrow. Fixing his eye on Dong Cheng, he loosed it with a hiss straight into the man’s back. Dong Cheng’s feet flew from the stirrups, and he tumbled headlong from his horse with a thud. Lu Junyi and the others signaled their troops and swept forward in a massed assault. Shen Ji was run through and killed by a thrust from Dong Ping’s spear. More than half the troops of Lingchuan were slain, and the rest fled in all directions. The commanders led their troops into the city together. Li Kui the Black Whirlwind was still in a murderous fury, hacking at everyone in his path. Lu Junyi repeatedly called out, “Brother, do not harm the common people!” Only then did Li Kui consent to stop.

p.src: Lu Junyi asked Geng Gong about the number of troops and commanders in the city of Gaizhou. Geng Gong replied, “Gaizhou is defended by a large force under Privy Councillor Niu. Yangcheng and Shenshui both lie west of Gaizhou, but Gaoping County is only about sixty li from here. This very night I want you to undertake a deed of merit for me. You must not refuse.” Geng Gong replied, “After receiving such great kindness from you, Vanguard, how could I fail to devote myself utterly?” Junyi said with delight, “Since you are willing to go, I shall assign several of my brothers to accompany you, together with the officers formerly under your command. Follow my instructions exactly, and I must trouble you to set out at once.” He then summoned the six or seven newly surrendered officers, rewarded each with food, wine, and silver, and promised them further rich rewards when the mission succeeded. When the drinking was over, Lu Junyi ordered Li Kui, Bao Xu, and five other infantry leaders, together with one hundred foot soldiers, to change into the armor and uniforms of Lingchuan troops and carry their banners. p.src: Once the assignments had been settled, Geng Gong and the others led the stratagem out of the city. The sun was already setting, and by the time they reached the southern gate of Gaoping, dusk had fallen. By starlight they saw dense ranks of banners upon the walls and heard the watch drums sounding with strict regularity inside the city. Reaching the foot of the wall, Geng Gong shouted, “I am Geng Gong, commander of the garrison at Lingchuan. Generals Dong and Shen refused to heed my words, opened the gate, and took the enemy lightly, thereby losing the city. I hastily took these hundred-odd men, slipped out through the northern gate, and came here by a bypath. Quickly let me into the city!” The guards shone torches down, recognized him, and hurried to inform Zhang Li and Zhao Neng. Zhang Li and Zhao Neng personally climbed the gate tower, while soldiers held several torches that cast light before and behind them. Zhang Li called down to Geng Gong, “Though you are our own men, we must still have a clear look at you.” Peering carefully downward, they saw that it truly was Geng Gong of Lingchuan, leading more than a hundred soldiers; their uniforms and banners were correct in every detail. Many soldiers upon the wall recognized the officers and pointed, saying, “That one is Sun Ruhu.” Then they said, “And that one is Li Qinlong.” Zhang Li laughed and said, “Let them in!” The city gate opened and the drawbridge was lowered. Then thirty or forty soldiers were ordered to secure both sides of the bridge before Geng Gong was finally admitted. The soldiers behind him surged forward in a mass, crying, “Quickly, get inside! Quickly, get inside! They are pursuing us from behind!” Paying no heed even to General Geng, the gate guards shouted, “What sort of place do you think this is? Why are you rushing about in such disorder?” While they were still jostling and disputing there, flames suddenly rose beside the spur of Mount Hanwang, and a body of cavalry swept out. Two commanders rode at its head, shouting, “Enemy general, do not flee!” Hidden among Geng Gong’s soldiers were seven fierce tigers: Li Kui, Bao Xu, Xiang Chong, Li Gun, Liu Tang, Yang Xiong, and Shi Xiu. At once they each drew their weapons and raised a battle cry; all hundred-odd men sprang into action together and stormed into the city. Those inside were caught unprepared and had no chance to shut the gate. Dozens of soldiers inside and outside the gate were soon cut down, and the attackers seized the entrance. Zhang Li cried out in dismay again and again, then hurried down from the wall with his spear leveled to seek Geng Gong, only to run straight into Shi Xiu. After exchanging several bouts, Zhang Li lost all desire to continue fighting and turned to flee, dragging his spear. Li Kui overtook him and, with one whistling stroke of his axe, chopped him in two. Meanwhile, the body of troops from the spur of Mount Hanwang sped to the city and surged inside. They were Shi Jin and Yang Zhi, who split up to pursue and kill the northern troops. Zhao Neng was killed amid the melee. More than half the Gaoping troops were slain, and Zhang Li’s entire household, old and young, was put to death. The townspeople, startled awake from their sleep, wailed so loudly that their cries shook the heavens. Presently Vanguard Lu also arrived with his army. He ordered every gate secured and sent more than a dozen soldiers through the streets to proclaim that the common people were not to be harmed. At daybreak, proclamations were posted to reassure the people, rewards were bestowed upon the soldiers, and a messenger was dispatched at full speed to inform Vanguard Song.

p.src: But let us waste no more words on this. We now return to Song Jiang’s army, encamped outside Weizhou. Vanguard Song was discussing affairs in his command tent when word suddenly came that Vanguard Lu had sent a messenger rushing with news of victory, together with a request that Vanguard Song reconsider their strategy for the next advance. Song Jiang was overjoyed and said to Wu Yong, “Vanguard Lu has captured two cities in as many days. The rebels have lost heart.” As he spoke, scouts from two different routes arrived to report, “The troops besieging Huixian and Wushe heard that Lingchuan had fallen, and both forces have lifted their sieges and withdrawn.” Song Jiang said to Wu Yong, “Your divine foresight, Master Strategist, is rarely equaled in any age!” He wished to strike camp and march west to unite his forces with Vanguard Lu’s and plan their next advance. Wu Yong said, “Weizhou has the Mengmen Mountains on its left and the Taihang Mountains on its right; to the south it borders the Yellow River, while to the west it commands Shangdang. It occupies a vital strategic position. If the rebels learn that our main army has gone west and send troops south from Zhaode, leaving our eastern and western forces unable to support one another, what shall we do?” Song Jiang said, “Your counsel is entirely right!” He therefore ordered Guan Sheng, Huyan Zhuo, and Gongsun Sheng to hold Weizhou with five thousand troops. He further commanded the naval leaders Li Jun, the two Zhangs, the three Ruans, and the two Tongs to lead the fleet and moor together on the Wei River, so that they and the defenders within the city might support each other like the two horns of a formation. Once the assignments were settled, the commanders accepted their orders and departed.

p.src: Song Jiang and his commanders led the main army, struck camp, and set out that very day. Nothing of note occurred along the road. When they reached Gaoping, Lu Junyi and the others came out of the city to welcome them. Song Jiang said, “Brothers, you have captured two cities in succession and rendered no small service. Every achievement shall be recorded in the register of merit.” Lu Junyi brought forward the newly surrendered commander Geng Gong to pay his respects. Song Jiang said, “General, you have forsaken evil and returned to the righteous path. Now that you will serve the state together with us, the imperial court will surely put you to important use.” Geng Gong bowed in thanks and stood in attendance. As his forces were too numerous to enter the city conveniently, Song Jiang made camp outside the walls. That same day, he consulted Wu Yong and Lu Junyi about which prefecture or district they should attack next. Wu Yong said, “Gaizhou has high mountains and deep ravines, and its roads are steep and difficult. Now that we have captured two of its subordinate counties, it stands isolated. We should first take Gaizhou to divide the enemy’s strength. Then, splitting our army into two routes and attacking from both sides, we can capture Weisheng.” Song Jiang said, “Your proposal, Master, accords exactly with my own thoughts.” He sent orders for Chai Jin and Li Ying to guard Lingchuan and relieve Hua Rong and the other six commanders so that they might come and serve with the main army, while Shi Jin and Mu Hong were to guard Gaoping. Chai Jin and the other three accepted their orders and departed. Then Zhang Qing, the “Featherless Arrow,” reported, “For the past two days I have been suffering from a chill. I wish to remain in Gaoping for a time to recuperate, and once recovered I shall report to camp for duty.” Song Jiang therefore ordered An Daoquan, the “Divine Physician,” to accompany Zhang Qing to Gaoping and treat him.

As his forces were too numerous to enter the city conveniently, Song Jiang made camp outside the walls.
That same day, he consulted Wu Yong and Lu Junyi about which prefecture or district they should attack next.
Wu Yong said, “Gaizhou has high mountains and deep ravines, and its roads are steep and difficult. Now that we have captured two of its subordinate counties, it stands isolated.
We should first take Gaizhou to divide the enemy’s strength. Then, splitting our army into two routes and attacking from both sides, we can capture Weisheng.”
Song Jiang said, “Your proposal, Master, accords exactly with my own thoughts.”

He sent orders for Chai Jin and Li Ying to guard Lingchuan and relieve Hua Rong and the other six commanders so that they might come and serve with the main army, while Shi Jin and Mu Hong were to guard Gaoping.
Chai Jin and the other three accepted their orders and departed.

Then Zhang Qing, the “Featherless Arrow,” reported, “For the past two days I have been suffering from a chill. I wish to remain in Gaoping for a time to recuperate, and once recovered I shall report to camp for duty.”
Song Jiang therefore ordered An Daoquan, the “Divine Physician,” to accompany Zhang Qing to Gaoping and treat him.
